title: Abu Nowas and the Three Scholars

full_text:
The celebrated poet Abu Nowas was walking through the academy quarter of Baghdad one sunny afternoon when he encountered three young scholars sitting beside a fountain, wearing new student turbans and boasting loudly of their mastery of grammar, logic, and poetic rhetoric.

Seeing the famous poet approaching in his simple woollen robe, the three students resolved to test his reputation and mock his casual attire.

The first student bowed with exaggerated courtesy: 'Peace be upon you, venerable elder! We are testing the three branches of poetic eloquence. Can you tell us why the moon appears silver while the sun shines golden?'

Abu Nowas smiled with amusement and answered: 'The sun shines with the golden fire of active labor, which builds cities by day; while the moon reflects the silver peace of meditation, which rests the soul by night.'

The second student stepped forward, smirking: 'And tell us, O master, which is swifter: the flight of an arrow, the speed of lightning, or the tongue of a scholar?'

Abu Nowas replied without hesitation: 'None of these, my young friend. The swiftest thing in all creation is the thought of an honest man turning toward truth, for it spans the distance from earth to heaven in less than a heartbeat.'

The third student, frustrated by their failure to confound the poet, asked with haughty disdain: 'And what is the heaviest burden that an educated youth can carry upon his shoulders?'

Abu Nowas looked him gently in the eye, adjusted his mantle, and said with quiet authority: 'The heaviest burden a youth can bear is a head inflated with unearned pride, for it blinds his eyes to wisdom, deafens his ears to counsel, and makes his feet stumble on the smoothest road.'

The three scholars blushed with deep shame, recognized their foolish arrogance, and bowed low before the master poet, thanking him for the lesson in humility that no classroom could teach.
moral: A sharp mind must always be tempered by humility, for youthful arrogance will inevitably meet its master.
